# Brian Hong

> Senior Salesforce Administrator, RevOps specialist, and Salesforce consultant based in Columbus, Ohio, with 12 years in the Salesforce ecosystem and 6 active Salesforce certifications. Available for full-time roles (Senior Salesforce Administrator, Salesforce Manager, Revenue Operations) and contract or consulting projects. Works remotely or hybrid in Columbus, OH.

Brian automates manual processes, fixes data quality, and sets up governance and Centers of Excellence so sales and service teams can spend their time on customers. He has supported orgs from 200 users to 60,000+ users across enterprise SaaS, ed tech, supply chain, logistics, and nonprofits.

## Key facts

- Name: Brian Hong
- Location: Columbus, Ohio, USA (serves Columbus metro, Ohio, and clients nationwide; mostly remote)
- Current role: Consultant, Talution Group (2026 to present)
- Experience: 12 years in Salesforce (2014 to present)
- Availability: Open to full-time roles and contract/consulting work

## Services

- Full-time: Senior Salesforce Administrator, Salesforce Manager, or Revenue Operations; building and leading a Salesforce Center of Excellence

## Expertise

- Sales Cloud: Lead-to-Opportunity automation with Salesloft, CPQ approval workflows and product rules, Slack alerts for MQL assignment and stage changes (40% less manual entry)
- Service Cloud: migration from Live Agent Chat to Messaging, queue consolidation, escalation rules, automated spam case blocking (+25% CSAT, 25% faster critical cases)
- Revenue Operations: validation tying Closed Won deals to POs and order forms, Einstein Activity Capture, data stewardship across Opportunity and CPQ objects (100% Closed Won audit alignment)
- Go-to-market support: campaign members routed to Salesloft cadences, reports delivered to Slack, cases synced to Jira via Celigo (30% less manual effort)
- Tools: Flow Builder, Screen Flows, Omni-Channel, CPQ, Data Loader, Workbench, SOQL, Permission Sets, Copado, Flosum, Jira, Slack, Okta SSO, Celigo, Zapier, DocuSign, Salesloft, Outreach, Clari, 6sense

- Interos, Associate Salesforce Program Analyst (2021 to 2022). Supply chain. 200+ users, 2 orgs. Consolidated flows and retired redundant automation.
- Salesforce, Contractor to Techforce Analyst to System Specialist I (2014 to 2021). Enterprise SaaS. 60K+ users, 6 orgs. Led M&A transitions onto internal IT; intake flows cut turnaround time by 20%.

## Case studies

- Scholarship and donor CRM automation (nonprofit, pro bono): 3-year engagement automating applications, integrating donations, and adding self-service forms. Result: 95% less manual entry, 90% fewer status emails.
- Service Cloud and Messaging overhaul (ed tech): consolidated queues, migrated to Messaging, blocked spam cases, synced escalations to Jira. Result: 25% faster critical cases, +25% CSAT.
- CPQ and quote-to-cash controls (ed tech and supply chain): CPQ bundles, product rules, approval workflows, and Closed Won validation. Result: 100% Closed Won audit alignment.

- [Salesforce duplicate management: matching rules that actually work](https://brianhong.com/salesforce-duplicate-management.html): Field note on data quality. Matching rules vs. duplicate rules vs. duplicate jobs, why standard matching rules miss duplicates and over-match, fuzzy matching methods and thresholds (First Name, Last Name, Company Name, Phone, Street, City, ZIP, Title), designing rules from a sample of real duplicates, Account domain, Contact, Lead, and Lead-to-Contact matching rule recipes, an alert-report-block rollout, entry points that skip duplicate rules (lead conversion, Quick Create, Undelete, API and DuplicateRuleHeader), duplicate jobs and merge survivorship, SOQL on DuplicateRecordSet for metrics, and a 30-60-90 day plan
- [Salesforce lead routing and speed-to-lead: a RevOps playbook](https://brianhong.com/salesforce-lead-routing.html): Field note on RevOps. What lead routing covers, why leads stall between marketing and sales, assignment rules vs. Flow vs. routing tools, MQL and ownership decisions, handoff to Salesloft or Outreach cadences, Slack alerts, measuring speed-to-lead, and a 30-60-90 day plan

What quote-to-cash covers, signs the data can't be trusted, tracing a deal end to end, CPQ bundles, product rules and approvals, gating Closed Won on the PO and order form, stewardship of opportunity data, an audit scorecard, and a 30-60-90 day plan

Audience brief, before and after, information architecture with 301 redirects, an OKLCH color and type system, hand-built HTML without a framework, structured data and llms.txt, and accessibility details
- [Standing up a Salesforce Center of Excellence from scratch](https://brianhong.com/center-of-excellence.html): Field note on governance. Decision rights, operating models, the intake-prioritize-release-measure loop, architecture guardrails, environments, KPIs, and a 90-day plan
- [Salesforce data stewardship is a people problem first](https://brianhong.com/data-stewardship.html): Field note on data quality. Owner, steward, and custodian roles, why fields go empty, critical data elements, stage-gated requirements, a weekly review habit, metrics, and a 60-day plan
- [Migrating Workflow Rules and Process Builder to Flow without breaking the org](https://brianhong.com/salesforce-flow-migration.html): Field note on automation. What end of support means, inventorying rules and processes, retire-consolidate-rebuild decisions, limits of the Migrate to Flow tool, how old concepts map to Flow, behavior changes, testing and cutover, and a 12-week plan
- [Salesforce data readiness for AI: what to fix before you turn on Agentforce](https://brianhong.com/salesforce-data-readiness-for-ai.html): Field note on AI. What data readiness for AI means, why agents expose data problems reports hid, six traits of AI-ready data, structured data and metadata, Knowledge and unstructured data, agent permissions, a per-use-case scorecard, and a 30-60-90 day plan

What a Salesforce tech debt audit is, where technical debt comes from, signs an org needs an audit, seven areas to inventory, free tools including Org Check and Code Analyzer, a risk-drag-effort scoring model, retire-consolidate-refactor-accept decisions, what to retire first, safe deletion steps, making the case to leadership, and a 30-60-90 day plan

## Homicide Victim Support

- [Homicide Victim Support: Rights & Help for Families of Murder Victims](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support): A plain-language guide for families after a homicide, written for every state. Covers victims' rights, the stages of a criminal case from investigation to parole, crime victim compensation and restitution, first-week steps, and national hotlines and organizations. In-depth guides for California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Texas are live. General information, not legal advice; Brian is not an attorney.
- [Federal vs. State Victims' Rights in a Murder Case: Which Law Applies?](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/which-rights-apply): Explains why state law, not federal law, governs nearly every homicide case, and compares victims' rights under the federal Crime Victims' Rights Act (18 U.S.C. 3771) with Ohio (Const. art. I, sec. 10a; R.C. ch. 2930) and Oregon (Const. art. I, secs. 42 and 43; ORS ch. 147), right by right with citations. Also covers what to do when a right is ignored.
- [Ohio Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Marsy's Law)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/ohio): A plain-language guide to Ohio victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Marsy's Law (Ohio Const. art. I, sec. 10a, effective 2018) and R.C. Chapter 2930 as revised by H.B. 343 (2023). Lists the ten constitutional rights plus a support person (R.C. 2930.09), the request-form waiver rule (R.C. 2930.04), the steps to take when a right is ignored and the 14-day and 30-day appeal deadlines (R.C. 2930.19; State v. Barnes, 2026-Ohio-2750), the Ohio Crime Victims Compensation Program ($50,000 total, $7,500 funeral, three-year filing; R.C. 2743.51 to 2743.72), no limitation on murder (R.C. 2901.13), full parole board hearings on request (R.C. 5149.101), and who to call in Ohio, including the Attorney General's victim services, the Ohio Crime Victim Justice Center, and ODRC victim notification.
- [Oregon Crime Victims' Rights for Homicide Families (ORS 147)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/oregon): A plain-language guide to Oregon victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Oregon Const. art. I, secs. 42 and 43 (adopted 1999, Section 42 amended 2008) and ORS Chapter 147. Lists eight rights, several of which depend on a request, the claim process at ORS 147.500 to 147.550 and its 35 day motion deadline (ORS 147.522), the Oregon Crime Victims' Compensation Program (ORS 147.005 to 147.367), and who to call in Oregon, including the DOJ Crime Victim and Survivor Services Division, the Oregon Crime Victims Law Center, and Department of Corrections victim services.
- [California Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Marsy's Law)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/california): A plain-language guide to California victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Marsy's Law (Cal. Const. art. I, sec. 28, Proposition 9, 2008). Covers the 17 enumerated rights and who counts as a victim (spouse, parents, children, siblings), enforcement in the trial or appellate court as a matter of right (sec. 28(c)), the next of kin's right to be heard at sentencing (Penal Code 1191.1), parole hearing notice and the 15, 10, 7, 5 and 3 year denial periods (Penal Code 3043 and 3041.5), the Board of Parole Hearings' commutation and resentencing reviews in effect as of October 2026 (15 CCR 2840 to 2859), CalVCB compensation and its filing period (Gov. Code 13953), no limitation on murder (Penal Code 799), and who to call in California.
- [Texas Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Chapter 56A)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/texas): A plain-language guide to Texas victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Tex. Const. art. I, sec. 30 and Code of Criminal Procedure Chapter 56A. Covers who counts as a close relative of a deceased victim (Art. 56A.001), the rights and their request requirements, standing to enforce but not to act as a party (Art. 56A.054), the family's statement after sentence is pronounced (Art. 42.03), one in-person representative at parole (Gov't Code 508.153), the Attorney General's Crime Victims' Compensation Program (Chapter 56B), the Texas Rangers' Unsolved Crimes Investigation Program, and who to call in Texas.
- [Florida Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Marsy's Law)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/florida): A plain-language guide to Florida victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Marsy's Law (Fla. Const. art. I, sec. 16(b) to (e), 2018). Covers rights that begin at the time of the crime, attending proceedings even as a witness, enforcement as a matter of right (sec. 16(c)), the statement at sentencing (Fla. Stat. 921.143), speedy trial demands and appeal deadlines, the 2023 Florida Supreme Court ruling that Marsy's Law does not keep a victim's name confidential, crime victim compensation under Chapter 960, parole after its 1983 abolition, and who to call in Florida.
- [Illinois Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Art. I, Sec. 8.1)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/illinois): A plain-language guide to Illinois victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Ill. Const. art. I, sec. 8.1 (2014) and the Rights of Crime Victims and Witnesses Act (725 ILCS 120). Covers the two representatives of a deceased victim (120/3), the free police report and 48-hour written rights notice (120/4), plea consultation, the written notice of assertion of rights and the enforcement procedure with appeal (120/4.5(c-5)), the Attorney General's victims' rights complaint process, the statement at sentencing (120/6), compensation under 740 ILCS 45 ($10,000 funeral, $45,000 total), youthful offender parole review (730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-115), and who to call in Illinois.
- [Pennsylvania Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Crime Victims Act)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/pennsylvania): A plain-language guide to Pennsylvania victims' rights for homicide victims' families under the Crime Victims Act (18 P.S. 11.101), as amended by Act 77 of 2022. Covers why the 2019 Marsy's Law amendment never took effect (League of Women Voters v. Degraffenreid, 2021), family members including step-relatives and a fiance (Section 103), the rights in Section 201, legal standing to enforce them (Section 231), mandatory restitution (18 Pa.C.S. 1106), PCCD compensation ($6,500 funeral, $35,000 total, five-year filing), no parole for life sentences (61 Pa.C.S. 6137), Commonwealth v. Lee (Pa. 2026) striking mandatory life without parole for second degree murder, the Office of Victim Advocate, and who to call in Pennsylvania.
- [Georgia Victims' Rights for Murder Victims' Families (Marsy's Law)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/georgia): A plain-language guide to Georgia victims' rights for homicide victims' families under Marsy's Law (Ga. Const. art. I, sec. I, para. XXX, 2018) and the Crime Victims' Bill of Rights (O.C.G.A. 17-17). Covers the order of relatives who count as the victim (17-17-3), plea input, defense interviews, blocking inmate mail, the 20-day motion that is the only enforcement route and is not appealable (17-17-15), impact testimony subject to cross-examination (17-10-1.2), compensation through CJCC ($6,000 funeral, $25,000 total), parole objections (17-17-13), and who to call in Georgia.
- [Victims' Rights and Compensation by State for Murder Victims' Families](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/compare-states): Side-by-side comparison of 25 states: Alabama, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and Washington. Crime victim compensation funeral limits (from $5,000 in Indiana, Missouri and Oregon to $12,818 in California), total caps (from $15,000 in Alabama, Indiana, Louisiana and South Carolina to $70,000 in California; no single overall cap in New York; North Carolina pays the funeral on top of $45,000 and Indiana on top of $15,000), filing deadlines (from 180 days in Indiana and South Carolina to seven years in California; none for death claims in Colorado since 2024), wrongful death deadlines, where each state's victims' rights come from (Marsy's Law in California, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina and Ohio; statute only in New York and Pennsylvania), how families enforce them, and parole in murder cases. More states are being added.
- [How to Write a Victim Impact Statement for a Murder Case (With Examples)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/impact-statement): A plain-language guide for homicide victims' families in any state to writing and giving a victim impact statement at sentencing. Covers what the statement is for, written and oral forms and having someone read it for you, what to include with example lines, what to leave out (including the capital-case limit from Bosse v. Oklahoma, 2016), questions to ask the victim advocate, and reusing the statement at parole. Cites the DOJ's victim impact statement guidance, Ohio R.C. 2930.14 and Oregon Const. art. I, sec. 42.
- [Open Homicide Investigation: What Families Can Expect](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/open-investigation): A plain-language guide for families in any state while a homicide is under investigation and no one has been arrested. Covers why detectives withhold details, what to ask for (one named contact, a check-in schedule, what may be said publicly), access to police records during an active investigation, when victims' rights begin, applying for compensation before an arrest, talking to the media, tips and rewards, and keeping a contact log.
- [Parole Hearings for Murder Victims' Families: What to Expect](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/parole-hearings): A plain-language guide for families in any state to parole hearings after a murder conviction. Covers when a sentence reaches parole, places that ended discretionary parole (including the federal system for crimes on or after November 1, 1987), registering for VINE and parole board notification, written, in-person and video statements, confidential statements, the POMC Parole Block Program, and release conditions. Cites 18 U.S.C. 3771(a)(4) and the U.S. Parole Commission.
- [Wrongful Death Lawsuit After a Murder: Deadlines in 25 States](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/wrongful-death): How a civil wrongful death lawsuit differs from the criminal prosecution (who brings it, standard of proof, who can be held responsible, cost), and the filing deadlines (statutes of limitations) in 25 states, the same 25 as the state comparison page, including homicide-specific rules (Cal. CCP 340.3, Fla. Stat. 95.11(11), 740 ILCS 180/2(e)), why Georgia's crime-victim tolling (O.C.G.A. 9-3-99) does not cover a family's claim, and shorter notice deadlines for claims against government agencies.
- [Vehicular Homicide & DUI Deaths: Rights for Victims' Families](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/vehicular-homicide): A plain-language guide for families of someone killed by a drunk, drugged or reckless driver. Explains that these deaths are homicides and the family are crime victims with victims' rights, and lists the main charge and statutory sentence in 25 states: Alabama (Ala. Code 13A-6-3 as amended effective October 1, 2026), Arizona (A.R.S. 13-1103), California (Pen. Code 191.5), Colorado (C.R.S. 18-3-106), Florida (316.193, 782.071), Georgia (O.C.G.A. 40-6-393), Illinois (625 ILCS 5/11-501(d)(1)(F), 720 ILCS 5/9-3), Indiana (I.C. 9-30-5-5), Kentucky (KRS 507.060), Louisiana (R.S. 14:32.1), Maryland (Crim. Law 2-503), Michigan (MCL 257.625(4)), Mississippi (63-11-30(5)), Missouri (RSMo 577.010), New Jersey (N.J.S.A. 2C:11-5), New York (Penal Law 125.12 to 125.14), North Carolina (N.C.G.S. 20-141.4), Ohio (R.C. 2903.06), Oregon (ORS 163.118 to 163.149), Pennsylvania (75 Pa.C.S. 3735), South Carolina (56-5-2945), Tennessee (T.C.A. 39-13-213), Texas (Penal Code 49.08), Virginia (18.2-36.1) and Washington (RCW 46.61.520). Covers why arrests are delayed by toxicology and crash reconstruction, pleas, shorter sentences and release notification, what happens when the driver also died or fled, crime victim compensation for drunk driving deaths (34 U.S.C. 20102), insurance, dram shop and social host liability, the bankruptcy exception for intoxicated driving deaths (11 U.S.C. 523(a)(9)), and the MADD Victim Help Line.
- [Slayer Rule: Can a Killer Inherit or Collect Life Insurance?](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/slayer-rule): A plain-language guide for families when the person who killed is a spouse, child, parent or other relative. Explains the slayer rule (a person who feloniously and intentionally kills someone is treated as having died first and cannot inherit, collect life insurance or take jointly owned property), its origins (Mutual Life v. Armstrong, 1886; Riggs v. Palmer, N.Y. 1889; Uniform Probate Code 2-803), and the law in 25 states: Alabama (Ala. Code 43-8-253 as amended by Act 2026-287, S.B. 41, effective October 1, 2026), Arizona (A.R.S. 14-2803, which includes manslaughter), California (Prob. Code 250 to 259), Colorado (C.R.S. 15-11-803), Florida (732.802), Georgia (O.C.G.A. 53-1-5, clear and convincing evidence without a conviction; 33-25-13 for life insurance), Illinois (755 ILCS 5/2-6), Indiana (I.C. 29-1-2-12.1), Kentucky (KRS 381.280, conviction required), Louisiana (Civ. Code arts. 941 and 946, R.S. 22:901), Maryland (Est. & Trusts 11-112), Michigan (MCL 700.2803), Mississippi (91-1-25, 91-5-33; Estate of Armstrong, 170 So. 3d 510, Miss. 2015, on insanity), Missouri (RSMo 461.054 and case law), New Jersey (N.J.S.A. 3B:7-1.1, 3B:7-6), New York (case law and EPTL 4-1.6), North Carolina (N.C.G.S. 31A-3 to 31A-12.1), Ohio (R.C. 2105.19), Oregon (ORS 112.455 to 112.555), Pennsylvania (20 Pa.C.S. ch. 88 as amended by Act 40 of 2024, including the escrow rule at 8814.1), South Carolina (62-2-803), Tennessee (T.C.A. 31-1-106), Texas (Estates Code 201.058, Insurance Code 1103.151, constructive trust under Bounds v. Caudle), Virginia (64.2-2500 to 64.2-2511) and Washington (RCW 11.84). Covers what happens without a conviction (civil finding by a preponderance of the evidence in most states), acquittals, manslaughter pleas, insanity verdicts, juveniles and murder-suicide; objecting to the killer as executor, freezing assets and written notice to banks and insurers; joint property; who takes instead; held life insurance claims and interpleader; ERISA plans (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, 2001; Laborers' Pension Fund v. Miscevic, 7th Cir. 2018; Standard Insurance Co. v. Guy, 6th Cir. 2024); Social Security survivor benefits (20 CFR 404.305(b)); SGLI and VA benefits (38 CFR 9.5(e), 38 CFR 3.11); who controls the funeral when the next of kin is charged; and crime victim compensation when the offender is family (34 U.S.C. 20102(b)(7)).
- [Cold Case Murders: What Families Can Do](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/cold-cases): A plain-language guide for families whose homicide case has gone cold. Covers written review requests, evidence retesting and forensic genetic genealogy (DOJ interim policy, 2019), the Homicide Victims' Families' Rights Act of 2021 (Pub. L. 117-164) for federally investigated murders on or after January 1, 1970, BJA's Prosecuting Cold Cases Using DNA program, NamUs for missing persons, keeping the case in public view, and keeping a family case file.
- [Checklist for Families After a Murder or Homicide (Every State)](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/checklist): A printable checklist for families after a homicide, written for any state and grouped by when things come up: the first few days, the first few weeks, the first few months, while the case moves, and the long road. Covers the medical examiner, death certificates, crime victim compensation, custody notification, plea consultation, victim impact statements, restitution, and parole notices.
- [What to Do After a Loved One Is Murdered: The First Two Weeks](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/first-two-weeks): A printable day-by-day checklist for the first fourteen days after a homicide, split into days one to three, days four to seven, and week two. Includes a fill-in record for the case number, detective, advocates, and claim numbers, and flags the five time-sensitive items: the compensation application, the written request for notice of proceedings, custody notification signup, employer leave paperwork, and the wrongful death statute of limitations.
- [Why I Built This Guide: My Mother and Brother's Murder in The Dalles, Oregon](https://brianhong.com/homicide-victim-support/why-this-exists): Brian Hong's personal account of why he built the guide. His mother, Patty Hong, and brother, Randy Hong, were murdered in The Dalles, Oregon on February 25, 2009. Covers what the family was never told (crime victim compensation and its deadline, property held as evidence, trial delays set by the defendant), why Ohio and Oregon are covered in depth, what the site is and is not, and how to reach Brian.
